claims.statement_en: Al-Kawthar is morphologically connected with abundance, and Arabic usage applies the term to anything great or plentiful in number, measure, or importance.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: والكوثر فوعل من الكثرة ... كل شيء كثير في العدد والقدر والخطر
claims.translation_review_note: aligned; English uses number, worth, and importance for the Arabic semantic range

claims.voice_position: Prophetic reports transmitted from Anas and Ibn Umar
claims.statement_en: One interpretation identifies al-Kawthar as a river in Paradise; the cited reports describe its precious banks and bed, pleasant soil, and exceptionally sweet and white water.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الأول أنه نهر في الجنة ... عن ابن عمر ... حافتاه من ذهب ومجراه على الدر والياقوت
claims.translation_review_note: aligned at retained proposition scope; the English covers river, Paradise, precious material, sweetness, and whiteness

claims.statement_en: A second interpretation identifies al-Kawthar with the Prophet's pool at the gathering; the cited report connects the promised river's abundant good with a pool visited by the community.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الثاني أنه حوض النبي ... قاله عطاء ... عليه خير كثير هو حوض ترد عليه أمتي
claims.translation_review_note: aligned at retained proposition scope; English pool/gathering coverage is present though ummah wording is not matched by the audit's community/nation probe

claims.statement_en: Ikrima identifies al-Kawthar as prophethood and the Book.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الثالث : أن الكوثر النبوة والكتاب ; قاله عكرمة
claims.translation_review_note: Book wording present in stored English; prophethood not established there

claims.statement_en: Al-Hasan identifies al-Kawthar as the Quran.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الرابع : القرآن ; قاله الحسن
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Al-Mughira identifies al-Kawthar as Islam.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الخامس : الإسلام ; حكاه المغيرة
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl identifies al-Kawthar as facilitation of the Quran and easing of the laws.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: السادس : تيسير القرآن وتخفيف الشرائع ; قاله الحسين بن الفضل
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.voice_position: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash and Yaman ibn Ri'ab
claims.statement_en: Abu Bakr ibn Ayyash and Yaman ibn Ri'ab identify al-Kawthar as the abundance of companions, the community, and followers.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: السابع : هو كثرة الأصحاب والأمة والأشياع ; قاله أبو بكر بن عياش ويمان بن رئاب
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Ibn Kaysan identifies al-Kawthar as altruistic preference.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الثامن : أنه الإيثار ; قاله ابن كيسان
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Al-Mawardi reports that al-Kawthar means elevation of remembrance.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: التاسع : أنه رفعة الذكر . حكاه الماوردي
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: An unnamed interpretation identifies al-Kawthar as a light in the Prophet's heart that guides him to God and cuts him off from all besides God.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: العاشر : أنه نور في قلبك دلك علي ، وقطعك عما سواي
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: A further report identifies al-Kawthar as intercession.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: وعنه : هو الشفاعة ; وهو الحادي عشر
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Al-Tha'labi reports an interpretation of al-Kawthar as miracles from the Lord by which those responding to the Prophet's call were guided.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: وقيل : معجزات الرب هدي بها أهل الإجابة لدعوتك ; حكاه الثعلبي ، وهو الثاني عشر
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Hilal ibn Yasaf identifies al-Kawthar as the testimony that there is no deity but God and Muhammad is the Messenger of God.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: الثالث عشر : قال هلال بن يساف : هو لا إله إلا الله محمد رسول الله
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: An unnamed interpretation identifies al-Kawthar as understanding of religion.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: وقيل : الفقه في الدين
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: An unnamed interpretation identifies al-Kawthar as the five prayers.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: وقيل : الصلوات الخمس ; وهما الرابع عشر والخامس عشر
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.statement_en: Ibn Ishaq identifies al-Kawthar as a great matter, supporting the lexical sense with a line of poetry.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: وقال ابن إسحاق : هو العظيم من الأمر
claims.translation_review_note: controlled research translation from Arabic; corresponding English meaning not established

claims.voice_position: al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas; Qatada, Ata, Ikrima; Anas; Said ibn Jubayr
claims.statement_en: The command to pray is variously explained as the obligatory prayer, the festival prayer on the Day of Sacrifice, and the dawn prayer at Muzdalifa; the sacrifice command is correspondingly linked with the rite, including slaughter after prayer.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: أقم الصلاة المفروضة ... صلاة العيد ويوم النحر ... صلاة الصبح المفروضة بجمع وانحر البدن بمنى
claims.translation_review_note: aligned across obligatory, festival, dawn/Muzdalifa, Mina, prayer, and sacrifice markers

claims.voice_position: Malik as reported by Ibn al-Arabi
claims.statement_en: Malik is reported as favoring the prayer of the Day of Sacrifice followed by the sacrifice, while acknowledging that he had received no transmitted statement on the verse.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: أما مالك فقال ما سمعت فيه شيئا والذي يقع في نفسي أن المراد بذلك صلاة يوم النحر والنحر بعدها
claims.translation_review_note: aligned, including Malik's no-transmitted-statement qualification

claims.voice_position: Ali, Muhammad ibn Kab, Ibn Abbas, Abu Salih and other named authorities
claims.statement_en: Competing non-slaughter readings connect wanhar with placing the right hand over the left at the upper chest, raising the hands in prayer, or facing the qibla with the chest; these are retained as attributed alternatives.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: ضع اليمنى على اليسرى حذاء النحر ... يرفع يديه ... استقبل القبلة بنحرك
claims.translation_review_note: aligned across hand placement, chest, hand raising, and qibla-facing markers

claims.voice_position: Qurtubi opening gloss and occasion report
claims.statement_en: Shani'aka is glossed as the one who hates the Prophet, first identified here with al-As ibn Wa'il; al-abtar is explained as the one cut off from good remembrance in this world and the next.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: أي مبغضك وهو العاص بن وائل ... المقطوع ذكره من خير الدنيا والآخرة
claims.translation_review_note: aligned across hater, al-As, cut-off, worldly, and afterlife meanings

claims.statement_en: Other reports identify Abu Jahl, Uqba ibn Abi Mu'ayt, or the hostile Quraysh context involving Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf, and another explanation treats the hostile group itself as cut off after claiming Muhammad had separated from them.
claims.evidence_anchor_ar: يعني بذلك أبا جهل ... هو عقبة بن أبي معيط ... لكعب بن الأشرف ... أنهم هم المبتورون
claims.translation_review_note: aligned; bounded English context explicitly contains Abu Jahl, Uqba, Quraysh, and Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf despite punctuation defeating the literal Ka'b marker
